title: Backend Reliability & Scale
goal: Learn the ten backend concepts from the supplied reading list through measurements, crash experiments and a reliable order pipeline.
outcomes: Explain p99 latency and fan-out amplification with explicit measurement assumptions.
Bound connection, worker, queue and retry budgets under overload.
Build durable idempotent operations and an atomic outbox with replay-safe consumers.
Read actual query plans and evaluate read gains against write amplification.
Simulate consistent hashing and observe real CDC snapshot, restart and recovery behavior.
studyGuidance: Suggested pace: six weeks at four to six hours per week; the guide groups the ten concepts and five labs into a study plan.
The supplied image is the topic checklist, not a technical authority. Each lesson links primary documentation or research.

Revisit the linked Database, Production Thinking and Networking lessons rather than repeating their introductory labs. JVM Internals is useful background for latency investigations but is not required.
Predict, experiment, save evidence, explain without notes, then implement a variation. Spend 25 minutes independently before asking AI for implementation.
Use existing notes for Prediction, Setup/version, Observation, Explanation, Evidence path, Remaining uncertainty and Revisit date.
Use local synthetic workloads with fixed bounds; record actual tool versions and use matching official documentation.
completionCriteria: Complete all ten concepts and answer their recall questions without notes.
Complete the five labs, including actual local CDC rather than only its simulation.
Verify every capstone acceptance criterion with repeatable correctness and recovery evidence.
Explain resource limits, uncertainty, replay guarantees and measurement limitations without notes.

topics.title: p99 latency and why averages hide slow requests
topics.description: Measure the slowest part of a request distribution and make the measurement boundary explicit.
learningGoals: Calculate mean, p50, p95 and p99 from raw samples.
Explain sampling, queue time and missing failed requests.
examples: A synthetic batch contains 9,800 requests at 10 ms and 200 at 1,000 ms.

tasks.title: Write a prediction and assumptions
Run the experiment and save evidence
Answer the recall questions without notes
Complete the independent practice and acceptance checks

material.explanation: A mean compresses all requests into one number, so rare long waits can disappear. A percentile is a threshold in a specified population and time window: p99 describes roughly the slowest one percent boundary, not the maximum. Define the estimator; for this lab sort N samples and use the value at one-based rank ceil(0.99 × N). Small samples make high percentiles unstable. Measure from scheduled arrival to completion when studying overload, including queue wait. Report errors, rejections and timeouts separately so a fast failure cannot masquerade as a fast successful response. Do not average instance p99 values to obtain a fleet p99; combine compatible histogram counts or raw samples. A client that waits for each response before sending the next request reduces offered load as the service slows and can conceal waiting that real arrivals would experience.

workedExample.scenario: A synthetic batch contains 9,800 requests at 10 ms and 200 at 1,000 ms.
steps: Nearest-rank p50 and p95 are 10 ms; p99 is 1,000 ms, and the maximum is also 1,000 ms in this constructed dataset.
A 200 ms objective fails for 2% of requests even though the mean looks comfortable.

commonMistakes: A p99 calculated from 50 requests is not a stable description of a large production population.
Discarding timeouts or averaging percentiles across servers biases the report.
guidedExercise: Create the 10,000 samples and calculate the sorted nearest-rank percentiles yourself.
Record the window, sample count, units and boundary; then add explicit timeout outcomes.
Compare scheduled arrivals with a caller that waits for the previous response.
material.independentExercise: Construct two datasets with the same mean and different p99 values. Explain which user experience each represents.
recallQuestions: Can two fleets have the same mean and different p99?
Why does a closed-loop caller hide overload?
How would you combine measurements from two instances?

acceptanceCriteria: Reproduce 29.8 ms mean and 1,000 ms p99 using the stated estimator.
Report sample size, failures and queue-time inclusion alongside the percentiles.

topics.title: Connection pooling and resource budgets
topics.description: Reuse connections while bounding pressure on the database and remote services.
learningGoals: Distinguish acquisition wait, connection establishment and operation timeouts.
Budget connections across replicas and keep transactions short.
examples: Three replicas each allow ten database connections, and each request holds one for 200 ms.

tasks.title: Write a prediction and assumptions
Run the experiment and save evidence
Answer the recall questions without notes
Complete the independent practice and acceptance checks

material.explanation: A pool lends reusable connections and limits simultaneous ownership. With HikariCP, closing a borrowed JDBC handle normally returns it to the pool; failing to close it leaves capacity occupied. maximumPoolSize bounds idle plus in-use connections, and connectionTimeout limits acquisition wait rather than SQL execution. A connection held while waiting on a remote API still consumes database capacity. Separate those calls from short database transactions when correctness allows. Plan a total connection budget across application replicas, background jobs, migrations and operational headroom. More connections can add database contention. HTTP reuse has different limits, especially with multiplexed streams; database pool settings do not configure an HTTP client. Use acquisition wait, occupancy and database utilization to locate the bottleneck before changing a size.

workedExample.scenario: Three replicas each allow ten database connections, and each request holds one for 200 ms.
steps: The application can consume 30 database connections before migration and admin headroom.
A ten-connection replica has an idealized ceiling near 10 / 0.2 = 50 operations/second if every request holds one throughout; contention and other bottlenecks can lower it.
Shorten measured hold time and compare equal offered load before raising the pool limit.

commonMistakes: A pool is not a rate limiter: ten fast calls can still produce high requests/second.
A new pool per request defeats reuse; an unclosed handle defeats availability.
guidedExercise: Revisit networking-unit-5 and use a shared JDBC pool capped at two connections in a disposable lab.
Start six bounded callers; record acquisition wait and active, idle and pending counts.
Compare a remote delay inside versus outside the transaction and verify all handles close.
material.independentExercise: Budget four replicas, a batch worker and an admin reserve against a database limit of 60; explain how rolling deployment overlap changes the budget.
recallQuestions: What does close mean on a borrowed JDBC connection?
Why can low database CPU coexist with pool timeouts?
Which timeout bounds query execution?

acceptanceCriteria: Show acquisition wait separately from query time and transaction duration.
Demonstrate capacity returning after success and failure, and document a replica-wide budget.

topics.title: Backpressure and bounded overload
topics.description: Make overload visible and keep accepted work within a finite resource budget.
learningGoals: Bound in-flight work and queued work.
Distinguish demand control, concurrency limits and rate limits.
examples: A worker finishes 20 jobs/second while arrivals sustain 50 jobs/second.

tasks.title: Write a prediction and assumptions
Run the experiment and save evidence
Answer the recall questions without notes
Complete the independent practice and acceptance checks

material.explanation: When producers add work faster than consumers finish it, a queue grows unless input slows, is rejected, or is durably deferred within a managed budget. Backpressure communicates consumer capacity upstream; a bounded queue plus an explicit rejection policy is one practical overload boundary. A concurrency cap limits simultaneous work, while a rate cap limits arrivals over time. Neither alone guarantees the other. Include waiting time in deadlines and cancel work that is no longer useful. Retries consume the same capacity and need capped attempts, backoff and jitter. A durable queue survives restarts but still needs retention, lag monitoring and an overload policy. Never silently discard accepted business work. Reactive demand is useful only if downstream buffering and work also respect the demand.

workedExample.scenario: A worker finishes 20 jobs/second while arrivals sustain 50 jobs/second.
steps: The backlog grows by about 30 jobs/second while those rates hold.
An initially empty queue with room for 120 waiting jobs fills in roughly four seconds, ignoring transients.
Bound active workers and queued jobs; record explicit rejection or durable deferral and verify recovery after the burst.

commonMistakes: An unbounded executor queue moves failure into memory and latency.
Immediate retries can increase the arrival rate exactly when capacity is lowest.
guidedExercise: Simulate arrivals and completions with a deterministic clock before adding threads.
Set worker count, queue capacity and deadline; count submitted, completed, rejected, expired and still outstanding jobs.
Slow the consumer, then restore it and measure oldest queued age and recovery time.
material.independentExercise: Design overload responses for an interactive read and an accepted order submission; explain when rejection is valid and what durable acceptance promises.
recallQuestions: How do rate and concurrency limits differ?
When does a queue absorb a burst rather than fix sustained overload?
What happens to cancelled queued work?

acceptanceCriteria: Show a hard bound on active plus queued work during a sustained overload run.
Account for every offered job and demonstrate recovery without an unlimited retry loop.

topics.title: Idempotency keys and ambiguous retries
topics.description: Make repeated attempts represent one durable business operation.
learningGoals: Define key scope, payload validation and retention.
Handle concurrent duplicates and a lost response without duplicate effects.
examples: An order commits but the response connection drops. The caller retries with the same scoped key.

tasks.title: Write a prediction and assumptions
Run the experiment and save evidence
Answer the recall questions without notes
Complete the independent practice and acceptance checks

material.explanation: An idempotency key names one caller intent across retries. It is not a hash-based excuse to merge two legitimate identical purchases. Scope the key by authenticated caller and operation, bind it to a canonical request fingerprint, and define the retention period. In a local database workflow, a uniqueness constraint arbitrates concurrent attempts; store the business change and replayable outcome atomically so a retry can recover the committed result. Reusing a key with different input must produce a defined conflict. Define how a simultaneous request observes in-progress work and how recovery works after a crash. A lost response does not prove a failed operation. Local atomicity cannot cover a remote provider: propagate a stable provider-supported key or reconcile the uncertain result. Deleting a key record too soon makes a late retry dangerous.

workedExample.scenario: An order commits but the response connection drops. The caller retries with the same scoped key.
steps: The first attempt stores the order and key outcome in one database transaction.
The retry finds the same fingerprint and returns the recorded order identity instead of creating another.
Two concurrent attempts use database uniqueness and transaction handling; a check-then-insert without a constraint is insufficient.

commonMistakes: Generating a fresh key for every retry creates new intents.
Recording success before an external side effect or after an unrelated transaction leaves a crash gap.
guidedExercise: Write a behavior table for first use, same payload, changed payload, concurrent use, crash before commit and response loss after commit.
Model a unique (caller_id, operation, key) record and a deterministic request fingerprint.
Run duplicate attempts concurrently and assert one order, then repeat after restarting the process.
material.independentExercise: Explain an expiry policy and a remote provider timeout. State which results are known, uncertain or retryable without inventing an exactly-once guarantee.
recallQuestions: Why does a request hash alone fail to express caller intent?
What if the same key has a different payload?
Which transaction owns the replayable outcome?

acceptanceCriteria: Concurrent identical attempts produce one durable local business effect and a stable outcome.
Changed payloads conflict and response-loss retries survive restart; external uncertainty is documented.

topics.title: Reading query plans with EXPLAIN ANALYZE
topics.description: Connect a slow query to measured row counts, loops and I/O.
learningGoals: Read a plan tree and compare estimated and actual row counts.
Validate a query or index change using equal inputs and write tradeoffs.
examples: A pending-order query is slow for a sparse tenant/status combination.

tasks.title: Write a prediction and assumptions
Run the experiment and save evidence
Answer the recall questions without notes
Complete the independent practice and acceptance checks

material.explanation: EXPLAIN shows a planner’s predicted strategy; EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement and adds measurements. Read the tree from data-producing children toward their parents. Costs are planner units, not milliseconds. Compare estimated rows with actual rows at the first large divergence. For repeated nodes, actual time and rows are per-loop averages, so inspect loops; parent times include child work and should not simply be summed. BUFFERS adds cache and I/O evidence, but a buffer read does not prove physical disk I/O because the operating system can cache it. A sequential scan may be the best choice for a small table or a broad match. Use representative distributions and refreshed statistics. Instrumentation adds overhead. Use disposable data: ANALYZE on a modifying statement really writes, takes locks and may trigger side effects; ROLLBACK does not undo every possible side effect such as sequence advances or external actions.

workedExample.scenario: A pending-order query is slow for a sparse tenant/status combination.
steps: Save EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) for the exact predicate and ordering on seeded data.
Find estimate/actual divergence, rows removed, repeated loop work and any sort or temporary I/O.
Test one candidate index or query change, refresh statistics, repeat equal inputs and compare read improvement with write cost.

commonMistakes: Seeing an index scan does not establish that a query is efficient.
Adding nested-node times double-counts included child work.
guidedExercise: Use the guide’s disposable SQL fixture to create a skewed 100,000-row order table.
Save baseline and candidate plans for the same tenant, status and LIMIT.
Try a broad filter and explain why the planner may prefer a scan; compare results as well as timings.
material.independentExercise: Investigate a join whose inner scan runs 10,000 times. Estimate total rows visited from per-loop values and propose one falsifiable change.
recallQuestions: What does loops change about actual rows?
When is a sequential scan reasonable?
Why is ANALYZE unsafe to try blindly on an UPDATE?

acceptanceCriteria: Annotate a real plan with estimates, actual rows, loops and buffer evidence.
Preserve query results and report a repeated comparison rather than one warm-cache timing.

topics.title: Write amplification and index tradeoffs
topics.description: Account for the physical work behind a small logical change.
learningGoals: Define the numerator and denominator of a write-amplification measurement.
Explain index, WAL, maintenance and storage-layer costs.
examples: A synthetic batch changes 1 MB of application payload and produces 8 MB of measured WAL delta.

tasks.title: Write a prediction and assumptions
Run the experiment and save evidence
Answer the recall questions without notes
Complete the independent practice and acceptance checks

material.explanation: A logical write can create multiple kinds of physical work: transaction log records, changed data pages, index maintenance and later cleanup. Define the layer before calculating amplification. WAL bytes per changed payload byte is a useful lab proxy, but it is not total device bytes written. Checkpoints, full-page images, caching, concurrent work and replicas complicate interpretation. PostgreSQL updates create new row versions; eligible heap-only tuple updates can avoid some index maintenance, subject to indexed-column and page-space conditions. Extra indexes can improve reads while increasing write and storage cost. In LSM-based engines, compaction rewrites data and trades write cost against read and space behavior; do not apply that implementation model indiscriminately to PostgreSQL. Compare equal logical work and preserve indexes required for correctness.

workedExample.scenario: A synthetic batch changes 1 MB of application payload and produces 8 MB of measured WAL delta.
steps: The defined WAL-to-payload proxy is 8× for this batch, not a claim about SSD-level write amplification.
Repeat equal batches on clean comparable fixtures with and without an optional status index.
Compare read plans, update throughput and WAL deltas; attribute differences cautiously and record checkpoint conditions.

commonMistakes: One SQL UPDATE is not one disk write.
Dropping a uniqueness index to win a benchmark can break correctness.
guidedExercise: Choose a fixed update count, payload width and transaction batch size on disposable data.
Measure WAL LSN delta on an otherwise quiet local database and label it as a proxy.
Compare indexed-column and non-indexed-column updates, and record table/index sizes and HOT statistics where available.
material.independentExercise: Propose the minimum index set for a write-heavy order status table. Defend each index against a concrete read or correctness requirement.
recallQuestions: What exactly does your amplification ratio measure?
Why can a read optimization harm writes?
How do HOT updates differ from LSM compaction?

acceptanceCriteria: Report logical work and WAL delta with units, repeat count and environmental limitations.
Explain one observed read/write tradeoff without treating the WAL proxy as device I/O.

topics.title: Consistent hashing and controlled key movement
topics.description: Map keys to changing owners without remapping the whole keyspace.
learningGoals: Implement deterministic ring ownership including wraparound.
Measure movement, balance and hotspots during membership changes.
examples: A ring has A=20, B=60 and C=90 in a toy 0–99 space. D joins at 40.

tasks.title: Write a prediction and assumptions
Run the experiment and save evidence
Answer the recall questions without notes
Complete the independent practice and acceptance checks

material.explanation: Modulo routing hash(key) % N can remap many keys when N changes. A consistent hash ring places keys and node tokens in the same ordered space; a key belongs to the first token clockwise, wrapping to the beginning. Adding a token changes ownership only in the interval it takes from a successor. Virtual nodes give a physical owner multiple token positions to improve distribution. They do not guarantee equal request load: one popular key can still dominate. Use deterministic encoding, hash function and collision tie-breaking across clients. Ownership is a routing decision, not data movement, replication, consensus or failure detection. A real membership change needs versioning, migration and a strategy for reads and writes during transition. A local simulation is enough to learn these boundaries.

workedExample.scenario: A ring has A=20, B=60 and C=90 in a toy 0–99 space. D joins at 40.
steps: Before the join, keys 25 and 35 belong to B; key 95 wraps to A.
After the join, keys in (20,40] move from B to D; key 50 remains on B.
Compare this deterministic movement with modulo routing over the same larger fixed key set, then add virtual nodes and measure distribution.

commonMistakes: A ring does not automatically copy data to its new owner.
Virtual nodes cannot split a single hot key’s traffic by themselves.
guidedExercise: Check exact-token and wraparound cases using the toy ring.
Map 10,000 fixed keys to three nodes, add a fourth, then remove a node; count changed owners.
Compare one token versus many tokens per physical node and a skewed request distribution.
material.independentExercise: Design a versioned cache membership transition and describe what happens when clients temporarily disagree on the owner.
recallQuestions: Which interval moves when D joins?
Why can balanced key counts hide an overloaded node?
What does hashing not solve about replication?

acceptanceCriteria: Deterministic boundary tests pass, including wraparound and token collision policy.
Report movement and load distribution, and distinguish mapping from actual migration.

topics.title: Change data capture: snapshots, logs and replay
topics.description: Build a recoverable projection from committed database changes.
learningGoals: Explain the snapshot-to-stream boundary and durable offsets.
Handle duplicate delivery, deletes, lag and schema changes.
examples: A consumer updates an order projection, then crashes before acknowledging the source position.

tasks.title: Write a prediction and assumptions
Run the experiment and save evidence
Answer the recall questions without notes
Complete the independent practice and acceptance checks

material.explanation: Change data capture exposes database changes to downstream readers. Log-based CDC can begin with a snapshot and continue from a coordinated log position so the initial data and later stream form a recoverable history. Track source position, commit boundaries and durable consumer checkpoints. A restart can replay changes that were emitted before an offset was saved, so consumers must tolerate duplicates. Apply a projection change and its deduplication/checkpoint state atomically when they share a database. Treat deletions and schema changes as explicit cases, and distinguish per-partition ordering from a global order. A lagging PostgreSQL replication slot can retain WAL and exhaust storage; retention limits can instead force recovery or a new snapshot. CDC transports row-level facts; it does not automatically identify the business intent behind several row updates.

workedExample.scenario: A consumer updates an order projection, then crashes before acknowledging the source position.
steps: On restart the source can deliver the same event again.
A stable event identity or suitable source-position strategy lets the consumer detect replay without incrementing totals twice.
Persist the projection effect and deduplication state together; if history is no longer retained, use a documented rebuild path.

commonMistakes: A table poll using only updated_at can miss ties or deletes and is not the same as log-based CDC.
Acknowledging before the durable effect risks lost processing; acknowledging afterward permits replay.
guidedExercise: First simulate an event stream with stable IDs, source positions, updates, a delete and a duplicate.
Build a projection and restart the consumer at an earlier checkpoint; assert the same final state.
For the real local CDC lab, inspect snapshot events, saved offsets, lag and replication-slot retention with the documentation for installed versions.
material.independentExercise: Plan a projection rebuild while writes continue. State how snapshot boundaries, ordering and incompatible schema changes are handled.
recallQuestions: Why do durable offsets not remove every duplicate?
What happens when a replication slot falls far behind?
How does a row update differ from a domain event?

acceptanceCriteria: A replayed update and delete produce the expected final projection after restart.
Explain snapshot handoff, lag monitoring, retention failure and recovery; distinguish simulation from real CDC.

topics.title: The transactional outbox pattern
topics.description: Commit business state and event intent together, then relay with replay protection.
learningGoals: Explain the database/broker dual-write failure.
Design atomic intent, at-least-once relay and idempotent consumption.
examples: An order and OrderCreated event commit; the relay publishes but crashes before saving its delivery marker.

tasks.title: Write a prediction and assumptions
Run the experiment and save evidence
Answer the recall questions without notes
Complete the independent practice and acceptance checks

material.explanation: Saving an order and separately publishing an event leaves a crash gap whichever action happens first. An outbox stores the business change and event intent in one database transaction. A polling relay or a CDC connector later publishes committed intent. The publish and local acknowledgement still span systems: a crash after publish but before marking delivery can cause a duplicate. Keep one event ID across attempts and make consumers deduplicate in the same transaction as their local effect. Use an aggregate key and version when per-entity ordering matters; multiple workers can reorder events unless the design prevents it. Define retry, poison-event handling, retention and replay. Outbox atomicity covers local state plus intent, not instantaneous remote effects. Polling is a valid first implementation; CDC is an alternative transport for the same intent.

workedExample.scenario: An order and OrderCreated event commit; the relay publishes but crashes before saving its delivery marker.
steps: Both local rows survive together because they share a transaction.
The relay retries the same event ID after recovery, so the consumer can receive two deliveries.
The consumer’s unique inbox entry and projection mutation commit together; the second delivery makes no second business change.

commonMistakes: Deleting or marking an event before confirmed publication can lose it.
A distributed lock alone does not make consumer effects idempotent.
guidedExercise: Draw crash points before commit, after commit, before publish, after publish and after acknowledgement.
Create business and outbox rows in one transaction; prove rollback removes both.
Replay an event into a consumer with a unique inbox key and atomic local effect.
material.independentExercise: Compare a polling relay with a CDC relay. Specify per-order ordering, poison-event recovery and the conditions under which old outbox rows can be removed.
recallQuestions: Which dual-write gap does the outbox close?
Why can a correctly implemented relay still deliver twice?
Where must the inbox record and business effect commit?

acceptanceCriteria: A failed local transaction leaves neither business state nor event intent.
Crashing after publish causes safe replay, with no missing event or duplicate consumer effect.

topics.title: Tail latency amplification in fan-out requests
topics.description: Predict how waiting for many dependencies changes end-to-end latency.
learningGoals: Calculate the probability that at least one required branch is slow.
Evaluate deadlines, partial responses and hedging under load.
examples: Each independent branch has a 99% chance of finishing within 100 ms; a parent needs all 100 branches.

tasks.title: Write a prediction and assumptions
Run the experiment and save evidence
Answer the recall questions without notes
Complete the independent practice and acceptance checks

material.explanation: A parallel request that waits for every branch completes at the slowest branch, plus coordination overhead. In a simple independent model, if each branch meets threshold T with probability p, all n branches meet it with probability p^n. This is a model for one threshold, not a formula that adds branch p99 values. Correlated failures, shared queues and common infrastructure change the distribution, so compare the model with traces. Serial dependencies accumulate time instead. Limit fan-out and pass a remaining end-to-end deadline through queueing and calls. Partial results may help when product semantics allow them. Hedging launches an extra attempt after a delay and can shorten some waits, but it consumes capacity, requires safe duplicate execution and cancellation, and may worsen overload.

workedExample.scenario: Each independent branch has a 99% chance of finishing within 100 ms; a parent needs all 100 branches.
steps: The probability all finish within 100 ms is 0.99^100, approximately 36.6%.
The probability at least one misses the threshold is about 63.4%; this is not a claim that the parent p99 is 100 ms.
Repeat with shared slow periods and compare results to expose the independence assumption.

commonMistakes: The p99 of a maximum is not the sum or average of branch p99 values.
Hedging slow writes without duplicate protection can duplicate side effects.
guidedExercise: Use a fixed-seed or deterministic simulation for fan-out widths 1, 10 and 100.
Compute predicted threshold misses, then compare independent and correlated slow branches.
Add a parent deadline, cancellation and a fan-out cap; report completed, partial, failed and cancelled outcomes.
material.independentExercise: Design a product-page request with inventory, recommendations and pricing. Decide which branches are required and whether any may return partial results.
recallQuestions: What assumptions justify p^n?
How do serial and parallel dependencies differ?
When could hedging make latency worse?

acceptanceCriteria: Reproduce the 63.4% threshold-miss calculation and label its independence assumption.
Measure parent latency separately from branch latency and demonstrate deadline/cancellation behavior.

material.explanation: Build a small local order intake and read model. Orders use scoped idempotency keys and an atomic outbox; a bounded relay sends events to an inbox-protected projection. Measure pool wait, request distributions and end-to-end projection lag. Use a deterministic hash-ring simulator for cache ownership and a bounded fan-out read simulator, rather than adding a real distributed cache just to demonstrate routing. Complete the separate real CDC exercise and compare it with the polling relay. The goal is a measured correctness argument across crashes, overload and recovery.

steps: Write invariants, request semantics, data model, resource budgets and crash matrix before implementation.

Publish a local runbook and explain which guarantees stop at the database boundary.

commonMistakes: Adding a broker or cache without a learning need expands infrastructure without proving correctness.
